content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the problem of fine-grained vision-language (VL) concept matching. Based on CLIP, the paper constructs a scenario that an image is connected to a subject-object-predicate triplet and asks the model to judge whether the match is reasonable. For solving this problem, a system is built upon LSeg, a CLIP-based segmentation model for extracting binary masks for the subject and object, and the improved cues are used for feature extraction and final prediction.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The studied problem is important for VL understanding.
2. The paper is easy to follow.

Weaknesses:

1. The studied scenario and method are superficial. Regarding the scenario, we understand that there are many complex scenes for VL understanding (and matching), but this paper constrains it within a simple scenario of subject-object-predicate triplets. Regarding the method, it relies on LSeg, a CLIP-based model, to extract object masks and visual features from the image.

This pipeline decomposes VL understanding (in particular, VL matching) into a quite superficial framework, that the subject, object, and relationship are all detectable in the image. This perfectly aligns with the data collection scheme (the data are constructed from the VG dataset -- for all data, the subject, object, and relationship clearly appear on the image. It is thus not surprising that the method works well on the collected data, but there are many cases that cannot be covered by this framework, e.g. there are multiple objects in the description, or either the subject/object is missing, or the description is abstract. To validate the ability on generalized scenarios, the method shall be evaluated on more challenging datasets such as the MS-COCO and Flickr30K image-text retrieval datasets, where image-to-text and text-to-image retrieval accuracy is computed. The point is, since the texts on these datasets are written by real users (not generated by triplet-based rules), the evaluation is more challenging and meaningful.

Overall, the method is based on a handcrafted pipeline (i.e. detection/segmentation -> feature extraction -> matching). It is highly limited to the proposed, simple scenario. No new insights have been introduced.

2. The method largely relies on CLIP pre-training and LSeg zero-shot segmentation. The examples shown in Figs 3 and 4 are quite simple (subjects and objects are clearly detected, background is somewhat clean, and there are no rare classes). I really doubt if the method can work well on a generalized scenario.

3. The authors seem unaware of some recent progress in this research field. For example, GLIP [Li et al., Grounded Language-Image Pre-training, CVPR22] has introduced a grounded method for pre-training VL models. I believe that many issues studied in this paper have been investigated in GLIP, but GLIP is not cited.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: good.

Quality: limited -- the evaluation is constrained within simple situations that do not fully challenge VL models (see above).

Novelty: limited, since the existence of region-based VL models, e.g. GLIP (yet the paper does not cite).

Reproducibility: looks fine -- LSeg is open-sourced, and the method is easy to implement.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper studied an interesting problem but proposed a rather superficial solution (in terms of both evaluation benchmark and algorithm). In addition, the authors seem unaware of recent progress in this community. I do not believe that the paper has achieved the publication standard of ICLR.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper tackles the spurious correlation issue in visual-language pretraining model like CLIP. The main idea is to disentangle the input image into subjects, objects and predicate and compute the fine-grained matching scores between visual components and word concepts. The proposed method can be plugged into a pretrained CLIP model without pretraining. The experimental results on Visual Genome and SVO-Probes show that the RelationCLIP outperforms the original CLIP.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

+The paper tackles an important problem in visual-language model and the proposed idea looks novel. 

+The proposed method can be used as a plug-and-play module and consistently improves the zero-shot performance on two datasets

Weakness

-It is not entirely clear how the subjects, objects and predicates are disentangled. Are they assumed to be known? 

-The method relies on Lang-Seg to predict the segmentation masks. How robust is the method to the errors in the predicted segmentation masks? 

-In the beginning of Section 3.3, the paper says that "We assume the causal structure to be known and consider three learned IMs". Is this assumption realistic in practice? 

-Would it be possible to evaluate the method on the same zero-shot classification benchmark (e.g., ImageNet) following CLIP? If no, the application of the method seems to be limited. 

-In practice, there could be multiple subjects and objects in an image. Is the method able to handle multiple subjects and objects?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is written well and easy to follow. To my knowledge, the approach is original too.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a new method to tackle the spurious correlation issue in visual-language models. The experiments show some promising results too. However, I found the method seems to be restricted to be applied in some specific scenarios where the subject, object and predicate are assumed to be known. This hinders the method to be used for many real-world problems. In addition, I think the approach should have been evaluated on the standard zero-shot classification benchmarks as CLIP does. Therefore, I would not recommend to accept this paper at this stage.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes the RelationCLIP, which disentangles the image into sub-images containing subject/object/predicate entities separately for Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining. A new dataset Visual Genome Concept of 5400 image-text pairs with (subject, verb, object) annotations is also proposed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- This paper proposes a new dataset Visual Genome Concept for CLIP evaluation.
- The proposed algorithm achieves superior results on the Visual Genome Concept and SVO-Probes.

Weaknesses:
- Limited Novelty. Disentangling the image into multiple sub-images or decomposing the sentence into objects/subjects/predicate entities may not be new in cross-modal learning , related works should be discussed, such as [i, ii, iii].
[i] Improving Description-Based Person Re-Identification by Multi-Granularity Image-Text Alignments, TIP 2020.
[ii] Fine-grained Video-Text Retrieval with Hierarchical Graph Reasoning, CVPR 2020.
[iii] Multi-Granularity Semantic Collaborative Reasoning Network for Visual Dialog, 2022.
- It lacks digital and deeper analysis on how the proposed method solves “Challenge 1: the pretrained language model in CLIP is biased and tends to rely on spurious relationships learned during pretraining.” Three examples in Fig.1 and Fig.3 may not be convincing enough. More statistical results/analyses should be added.
- Fig.2 is hard to understand. Maybe necessary arrows/symbol explanations should be added? And From fig.2 it is a bit confusing to understand “training-free”. It seems that the training framework is changed in RelationCLIP and the all networks should be trained to perform better than CLIP.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This Paper is not clear enough on some figures and demonstrations. The originality might be minor with using the image disentanglement in cross-modal learning. It is hard to identify the Reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this paper propose to disentangle the visual input into sub-images containing subject/object/predicate entities for CLIP.  Given the strengths(new dataset and effective relationCLIP) and weaknesses(lack of clear and convincing demonstrations, limited novelty ), I would recommend weak reject.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
